title: Check that value_string values are ascending

notes.body: assigned to @martin.r.mathieson

I do wonder if this is worth checking / encouraging?

If values are in order:
- it is easier to change over to _ext for faster lookup
- it might well make the code more consistent and easier to navigate

Reasons for wanting the values to be out of order:
- they may be out of order in the spec, so the current order might make sense
- if never going to move to _ext, putting more common values near the start could make the lookup faster

Agree with the pros/cons.  Is speed over "readability" the real question?  Not sure I like it, but what about an "exception list" for value_strings that are _intentionally_ out of order (to limit noise in the pipeline when doing this check)

There are around 540 ascending value_strings detected now across all dissectors (I fixed a couple to get a feel for it).  It won't show up in the pipeline, as hidden behind an 'extra' flag (that is enabled when called through check_dissector.py).

Could maybe create an exceptions list organically, by grumbling when I notice in recent commits, and adding them if there seems to be a good reason for it.

I was using "pipeline" as a "generic notice to developer(s)".  Could it be part of precommit check?  If it's just a "warning" in the pipeline, will it get noticed? (I know I've been guilty of not looking over pipeline output if it passes with "warnings" that really should be fixed in an MR) I just don't know how many of those 540 are "intentional" versus copy/paste/update inconsistency that should be fixed.  But yes, I presumed the exception list would rise organically.

I've updated a few more dissectors, definitely some were just accidentally out of order, but I believe others I looked at followed the order described outside the dissector. I could probably make it more focused by limiting the check to only consider value_strings with > (say) 10 entries, and only be interested if the backwards jump was less than (say) 10.
I haven't added any of my checking scripts to the git precommit check - checks either need to identify definite errors, or maybe-valid warnings will flash past then get hidden by the commit editor..
IMHO the order only really matters when using an extended value_string due to the way it works. It is not important for normal ones and could allow keeping the array aligned with a spec.

I was comfortable enough fixing the examples in this commit - if the values come from #defines or enums that were already in ascending order.

But yes, I'm not sure its really worth anyone's time to go through lots of these unless they were going to be changed to extended.

If *all* of the value_strings were in-order, the regular lookup could potentially be faster (either treated as extended, or just give up as soon as that value was passed), but doing that might not be faster, and there is no sensible way to make sure they are all in-order.  In any case, I only remember once when I profiled Wireshark did a value_string lookup catch my eye, and that was an extreme case.

If no-one objects, I'll merge this, but only consider the output for dissectors I am working on.
May be count the number of entry ? and set warning if more of X ? (and it is recommanded to use \_ext ?)

I'd thought about that before.  I would need to do some timing measurements to work out a sensible cutoff.  An 'ext' field does store a few more bytes (48?) in a val64_str_ext, and the tradeoff depends in part upon how often this lookup will need to be done.  The scan to work out which search is needed is done lazily on the first access.

Also, the benefit is greater (and at a smaller size) if the values allow for VS_INDEX than for VS_BIN_SEARCH.

The other thing that could be done is to identify existing 'ext' usages that will be falling back to VS_LIN_SEARCH, then look at them to either 'fix' them, or demote to value_string.
